required_edits.evidence_note: Fresh readings 2026-10-31, re-checked by independent review the same day. (1) McCallum, Innes and Hill, The Conversation (Canada), 1 July 2024, read in full. 'We began creating the historian profiles due to frustration with a lack of public engagement in Indigenous historical scholarship' (¶18). Noticing few Indigenous historians presenting research at professional history conferences, the authors 'chose to create a publishing and public information alternative that is Indigenous-led and focused' (¶¶23–24). 'Shekon Neechie editorial board members also published an open letter responding to the denial of colonial violence' (¶30). This is a community-controlled site, so the letter is paraphrased, not quoted. It is signed by the seven board members as 'Shekon Neechie Board', McCallum second and Innes seventh. It supports the CHA's Canada Day Statement on the term genocide, answers the open letter signed by fifty-three historians, and names no historian. The 2024 essay is a co-authored public explanation, not a research article. The edge records collaboration (co-founding, co-signing, co-authoring), not a claim that their scholarship shares one argument. verdicts.reason: The opening passage is verified word for word in the Semantic Scholar record for DOI 10.1353/aiq.2009.a362033 (publisher's first-page excerpt), including 'Philip Deloria argues …' and 'One of these frames is professional history.' This is an attributed opening-passage reading, which provenance rule 4 allows, and the claim is properly bounded to the framing paragraph. Direction (Deloria → McCallum, contribution) follows atlas usage for named uses of another scholar's argument (cf. Cronon → Deloria, edge_2616). Identity: the excerpt says only 'Philip Deloria'. Reading it as Philip J. Deloria rests on the subject: Indian modernity and the frames non-Indians use to 'explain and contain' Indians, which is the argument of Indians in Unexpected Places (2004). required_edits.evidence_note: Opening passage of the article (American Indian Quarterly 33:4, 2009, first page p. 523), read 2026-10-31 as the publisher's excerpt carried in the Semantic Scholar record for DOI 10.1353/aiq.2009.a362033; Project MUSE served a bot check. Re-checked by independent review. She writes that the article answered a Western History Association call for papers by Indigenous academics on 'working from home'. She wanted 'to make visible a division that separates Native people as history and Native people as historians', and to do so by historicizing 'the twentiethcentury English Canadian historical profession' [sic, as printed in the excerpt]. She continues: 'Philip Deloria argues that part of a project of understanding Indian modernity is to take as the subject of investigation the ideological and discursive frames non-Indians use to explain and contain Indian people. One of these frames is professional history.' The excerpt names neither the Deloria work nor his middle initial. He is identified as Philip J. Deloria, the historian of Indian modernity (Indians in Unexpected Places, 2004), from the subject of the sentence; that is an inference. The legal scholar Philip S. Deloria is a namesake. The rest of the article (pp. 524–544) is unread. This is a named use in her framing paragraph; no claim is made about how far the rest of the article depends on Deloria.

On p. 69 he says that following Turner's standardized questions and Henige's control of the interview 'would prove problematic' in Native Studies research. The critique kind has type critique, and the edge is distinct from Wheeler's edge_2179. required_edits.evidence_note: Gladue Rights Research Database record (University of Saskatchewan, with Legal Aid Saskatchewan and the Law Society of Saskatchewan): the excerpt of p. 64, and the attached PDF of the article (pp. 63–88), read 2026-10-31 for its method passages. On p. 64, Native Studies 'challenges the conventional historical methodologies' and 'also challenges the conventional oral historical methodology'. It 'rejects the hierarchical researcher-researched relationship', and the researcher must be 'flexible to accommodate the interviewee's mode of communication'. Excerpts from three veterans' interviews are used to show that 'conventional oral historical methodologies are problematic in an Aboriginal context'. On p. 65, Vansina's widely accepted definition of oral tradition 'tends to promote a static view of orally transmitted narratives'. The edge targets the field because the article's critique is of conventional oral-history method as practised by several scholars (Vansina, Henige, Turner), none of whom is an atlas endpoint. verdicts.reason: Verified in the University of Manitoba repository PDF. PDF p. 56, n. 15: 'For a good overview of treaties, the Indian Act, reserves, residential schools and Metis loss of lands see Frideres, Aboriginal Peoples in Canada; Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens; Dickason, Canada's First Nations'. PDF p. 133: colonial forces 'have not been military, as a rule, but rather, have been institutional through economic, religious, educational legislative, and media systems (Frideres, Ponting, Miller, Dickason, Green)'. Direction is right: Miller's work feeds LaRocque's argument, so Miller → LaRocque. Judgement on the researcher's question: a recommended-overview footnote and a five-name parenthetical are a thin but real citation-in-argument, not topic overlap. They are worth an edge because they show LaRocque using Miller as an authority while criticising other settler historians, and Miller has only two edges. The wording must be weaker than 'names Miller among the authorities for her argument', and the namesake risk must be recorded. Her bibliography also lists Christine Miller (co-editor of Women of the First Nations, 1997, which contains a LaRocque essay). The p. 133 parenthetical gives no title, so attributing it to J. R. Miller is an inference from context and from n. 15. The 'printed p. 130 by the page offset' claim cannot be checked (printed numbers are not in the text layer); cite PDF pages only.

required_edits.relationship: In her 1999 dissertation Emma LaRocque recommends Miller's Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989) as an overview of treaties, the Indian Act, reserves, residential schools and Métis land loss. She also cites 'Miller' with Frideres, Ponting, Dickason and Green for the point that colonial forces acting on Native peoples in Canada were institutional rather than military.
required_edits.map_label: Cited by LaRocque as overview and authority, 1999
required_edits.evidence_note: LaRocque, Native Writers Resisting Colonizing Practices in Canadian Historiography and Literature (PhD, University of Manitoba, 1999), University of Manitoba repository PDF, read 2026-10-31 at the passages concerned and re-checked by independent review (text layer; OCR slips corrected). PDF p. 56, n. 15: 'For a good overview of treaties, the Indian Act, reserves, residential schools and Metis loss of lands see Frideres, Aboriginal Peoples in Canada; Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens; Dickason, Canada's First Nations.' PDF p. 133: the colonial forces 'have not been military, as a rule, but rather, have been institutional through economic, religious, educational legislative, and media systems (Frideres, Ponting, Miller, Dickason, Green)'. That parenthetical gives no title. Her bibliography lists both 'Miller, J.R. Skyscrapers hide the heavens' (1989) and Christine Miller and Patricia Chuchryk, eds., Women of the First Nations (1997). Reading the p. 133 'Miller' as J. R. Miller is an inference from its context and from n. 15. This is a recommended overview and a citation in argument, not an endorsement of Miller's whole interpretation. LaRocque elsewhere criticises settler 'cross-cultural' historians (her edges to Van Kirk, Brown and Trigger), and Miller is not among those she names there. No Miller text read.

verdicts.reason: Judgement on teaching use: hold. The syllabus and reading list are verified. The Wayback capture of the UW PDF (the live URL is 404) assigns Silent Spring pp. 1–37, 103–27 and 187–98 for 'TOXIC POLITICS', 30 November 1994, and lists it as a bookstore text. The 2005 handout lists it first under 'Classics and Precursors'. But assigning a book in a seminar, or listing it as a classic, shows that a text belongs to the field's canon. That is exactly the claim of edge_912 (Carson → environmental history), which already cites both of these sources. As a person ↔ person edge it would assert a relationship with Cronon's own scholarship for which no Cronon text arguing from, crediting or engaging Carson has been found (the researcher says so). The cited precedent does not carry over. Leopold → Cronon (edge_1245) rests mainly on Cronon's named debt in the 2003 afterword (his landscape workshops 'were in fact modeled on a famous course taught by Aldo Leopold') and on his essays about Leopold; the reading list is corroboration there, not the basis. Adding this edge would turn the 2005 reading list's ten 'precursors' into potential person edges, and syllabus edges would multiply without showing intellectual debt. Revisit only if a Cronon text that engages Carson is read (e.g. an essay, foreword or lecture naming her as a model). The teaching evidence stays on edge_912.
